units.translation: the same construction as Theognis, compared by Blomfield, v. 223, said νόου βεβλαμμένος ἐσθλοῦ [deprived of his good sense].
πόλις [city]. On this usage see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1821.
and in an endless robe she strikes the man, having bound him in the cunning garment
but instead of the ancestral altar, she remains as a chopping block, struck with a hot bloody offering
who is so childish or so stricken in his wits?
I struck up the Arian dirge
Corax, one of the dogs of Actaeon
and standing over the body like a hostile raven
with unholy minds, like ravens that have no regard for altars
of Diana. Thus, as the meter demands, I corrected for Λατογένεια κούρα [Leto-born girl].
where I added the words Διὸς κόρα [daughter of Zeus] by conjecture.
κορᾶν [of girls] wrongly introduced for χοροῦ [of the dance]. See χορός [dance].
of what man or deep-girdled girl?
daughter of Zeus, and we call her Justice
you will learn everything briefly, daughter of Zeus
great indeed are the unhappy maidens of Night, honored with mourning
may the daughter of Zeus look upon me. (Artemis)
of warlike uproar, where the scholiast says ταραχαί · κεκωμῴδηται δὲ ἡ λέξις [disturbances; the word is ridiculed].
It is said not rarely of insolence arising from excessive satiety: see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1840.
i.e. insolently, as πρὸς βίαν [by force], πρὸς ἡδονήν [for pleasure] and other such phrases have the force of adverbs.
for there is no bulwark of wealth against satiety for a man who has kicked the great altar of Justice
and to make white hairs rise upon her through this disease

(with nominative plural κόρυμβα [tops]: see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1848.) the extremity of a ship, as in Hom. Il. 9, 241 στεῦται γὰρ νηῶν ἀποκόψειν ἄκρα κόρυμβα [for he threatens to cut off the topmost ornaments of the ships]

κόρυμβα [tops]: the things called by some ἄφλαστα [stern ornaments], the ἀκροστόλια [prow ornaments], the extremities of the sterns. The extremities of the ships, smoothed for adornment and curved, which are at the stern and at the prow
and shatters all the top-ornaments of the Phoenician ship
come, reach this topmost peak of the hill
for he threatens to cut off the topmost ornaments of the ships
if the matter is accomplished by the will of Zeus
he will adorn his father's house with spoils
to adorn these images with new votive tablets
I would not fear any man's adornment
